name: Lies, Lies, Lies

items.name: Insured against fright
items.fact: For the 1958 horror film Macabre, the director William Castle gave every cinemagoer a 1,000-dollar life-insurance policy from Lloyd's of London, in case they died of fright.

items.name: Buzzing seats
items.fact: For The Tingler (1959), some cinemas fitted small buzzers under the seats. At the scariest moment, they gave the audience a little shock.

items.name: The flying skeleton
items.fact: At screenings of House on Haunted Hill (1959), a plastic skeleton flew over the audience on a wire just as a skeleton appeared on screen.

items.name: No late arrivals
items.fact: For Psycho (1960), Alfred Hitchcock told cinemas not to let anyone in after the film had started, so nobody would miss the shock early in the film.

items.name: The telekinetic café
items.fact: To promote Carrie (2013), actors staged a scene in a New York café: a woman seemed to throw a man up a wall and move furniture with her mind. Hidden cameras filmed customers' reactions.

items.name: Chatroulette scares
items.fact: To promote The Last Exorcism (2010), the studio used Chatroulette, a random video-chat site. Strangers saw a young woman who suddenly seemed to become possessed.

items.name: Blood drives
items.fact: From Saw II (2005) onwards, the Saw horror films ran blood drives with the American Red Cross, asking fans to give blood. Tens of thousands of donations were made.

items.name: The banned trailer
items.fact: In 2018 YouTube removed an advert for the horror film The Nun because it was too shocking: it looked like the phone's volume being turned down, and then came a sudden jump scare.

items.name: Snakes on a Plane
items.fact: Before Snakes on a Plane (2006) came out, fans online made so many jokes about it that the studio filmed extra scenes, including a famous line fans had suggested.

items.name: Free sick bags
items.fact: For the horror film Mark of the Devil (1970), cinemas handed out free sick bags to the audience, with the promise that the film would upset their stomachs.

fakes.name: The candle street
fakes.fact: To promote a ghost film, a Spanish studio switched off the street lights on one Madrid street every night for a week, leaving one candle in each window.

fakes.name: The mirror tickets
fakes.fact: Every cinemagoer at a British horror film in 1963 got a small mirror to check behind them during the scariest scene.

fakes.name: The reopened cinemas
fakes.fact: A Japanese ghost film was shown only in old cinemas that had been closed for at least ten years and were reopened for one month.

fakes.name: The tape that deleted itself
fakes.fact: A German studio sent film critics a cassette of its new thriller that erased itself 24 hours after it was first played.

fakes.name: Free torches
fakes.fact: A Swedish horror film in 1984 gave a free torch with every ticket, to switch on if you got too scared. Many cinemas asked for the idea to stop.

fakes.name: The 3 a.m. challenge
fakes.fact: A Mexican studio offered free cinema tickets for life to anyone who watched its horror film alone, in an empty cinema, at three in the morning.

fakes.name: The tipping seats
fakes.fact: For a 1960s monster film, an American cinema chain fitted seats that tipped slightly backwards when the monster first appeared.

fakes.name: The trailer in the weather
fakes.fact: A Danish thriller's trailer was hidden inside a weather forecast on national TV: the map slowly filled with red fog.

fakes.name: Garlic popcorn
fakes.fact: To advertise a vampire film, a Hungarian cinema chain sold only tomato juice and garlic popcorn for its opening weekend.

fakes.name: The fading tickets
fakes.fact: A Korean horror film printed its tickets with ink that faded during the screening, leaving only the words “Don't look back.”

fake: Give the stunt a short name: “the … seats”, “the … tickets”.
What kind of film (horror, thriller, monster), a country and a year.
A studio, a director or a cinema chain (no real names).
One or two steps: what the audience saw or got.
Did it work? Did anyone complain?

tips: Be specific: numbers, dates and real places make a lie believable.
Give it a small problem (“some cinemas refused to do it”): perfect things sound fake.
Make both talks the same length and give them the same confidence.
